title: Gilgamesh: The Broken Epic
subtitle: Reading a 4,000-year-old story from pieces of clay

learningObjectives.text: How does the epic reach us?
Why does the fragmentary state matter?

pennsylvania.work: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
pennsylvania.author: Anonymous
pennsylvania.translator: Morris Jastrow and Albert T. Clay
pennsylvania.locator: Pennsylvania Tablet · Column III · part 1; Pennsylvania Tablet · Column III · part 1, normalized characters 115-785
pennsylvania.excerpt: Enkidu had not known To eat food. To drink wine He had not been taught. The woman opened her mouth and Spoke to Enkidu: "Eat food, O Enkidu, The provender of life! Drink wine, the custom of the land!" Enkidu ate food Till he was satiated. Wine he drank, Seven goblets. His spirit was loosened, he became hilarious. His heart became glad and His face shone. [The barber(?)] removed The hair on his body. He was anointed with oil. He became manlike. He put on a garment, He was like a man. He took his weapon; Lions he attacked, (so that) the night shepherds could rest. He plunged the dagger; Lions he overcame. The great [shepherds] lay down; Enkidu was their protector.
pennsylvania.note: Verbatim translation from the named Old Babylonian tablet witness in this edited edition. Brackets and question marks signal textual restoration or uncertainty.

yale.work: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
yale.author: Anonymous
yale.translator: Morris Jastrow and Albert T. Clay
yale.locator: Yale Tablet · Column IV; Yale Tablet · Column IV, normalized characters 0-1009
yale.excerpt: To keep safe [the cedar forest], [Enlil has decreed for it] seven-fold terror." Gish [opened] his mouth and spoke to [Enkidu]: "Whoever, my friend, overcomes (?) [terror(?)], it is well (for him) with Shamash for the length of [his days]. Mankind will speak of it at the gates. Wherever terror is to be faced, Thou, forsooth, art in fear of death. Thy prowess lacks strength. I will go before thee. Though thy mouth calls to me; "thou art afraid to approach." If I fall, I will establish my name. Gish, the corpse(?) of Huwawa, the terrible one, has snatched (?) from the time that My offspring was born in ...... The lion restrained (?) thee, all of which thou knowest. ........................ .............. thee and ................ open (?) ........ like a shepherd(?) ..... [When thou callest to me], thou afflictest my heart. I am determined [to enter] the cedar forest. I will, indeed, establish my name. [The work(?)], my friend, to the artisans I will entrust. [Weapons(?)] let them mould before us.

narrativeBlocks.title: Clay, not parchment
narrativeBlocks.body: Gilgamesh survives on baked clay tablets — cuneiform libraries buried when cities fell. The story you read was literally dug out of the dirt in the 19th century.

narrativeBlocks.title: A text made of shards
narrativeBlocks.body: No single tablet has the whole epic. Scholars assemble it from overlapping fragments across tablets and centuries — the Pennsylvania tablet, the Yale tablet, pieces from Ashurbanipal's library — each filling another's gaps.

narrativeBlocks.title: Older than Homer by miles
narrativeBlocks.body: The story predates the Iliad by over a thousand years — and the flood account inside it is older than the version in Genesis, raising the famous question of which tradition borrowed from which.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the gaps mean
narrativeBlocks.body: The fragments' broken edges aren't just damage — they are part of what the text IS now. You read an epic about loss, assembled out of pieces, about the one thing everyone in it most wants and cannot keep: life without end.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why read a broken thing?
narrativeBlocks.body: Because it still works. Gilgamesh's grief for Enkidu lands across 4,000 years through clay dust — proof that the story was good enough to survive being buried alive.

quiz.prompt: How does the Epic of Gilgamesh reach modern readers?

choices.text: A single complete manuscript in Babylon
Assembled from broken cuneiform tablets dug out of buried cities — overlapping fragments from different libraries

quiz.explanation: The epic is a jigsaw of shards — reading it is archaeology.

quiz.prompt: Why does the fragmentary state matter?

choices.text: The text's brokenness is part of its meaning — an epic about loss literally lost, recovered piece by piece

It makes the text shorter to read

quiz.explanation: The gaps are honest — a story about mortality that almost didn't survive its own.
